name: Buck Mountain, Static Peak and Albright Peak

legs.route: East Face, reached by the Stewart Draw climbers' trail

legs.connect: Drop from Buck onto the talus below and cross it to the base of Static's east ridge; the direct ridge between the two is much harder and most parties skip it.
Descend Static to the Alaska Basin trail junction, then follow a steep trail up Albright.

how: All three summits sit above one drainage and are strung into a loop from the Death Canyon trailhead. Buck comes first because it has the longest, most route-finding-heavy approach, via a faint trail into the draw and over talus to a high lake. The ground is mostly class 2 with a few class 3 moves and a lot of loose rock, and Buck's lower cliff bands must be bypassed by a gully or ledges. Static and Albright are easy by comparison. Static is also commonly paired with Albright alone, via the switchbacking trail to the divide.
descent: Return by the switchbacks of the Alaska Basin trail to the canyon trail and down past the lake to the trailhead. This avoids repeating the talus approach used on Buck.
logistics: Roughly 15 miles and 7,000 feet of gain for the full loop, with a short climb at the very end back to the trailhead. Social trails fade, so navigation matters; a snow-free late summer is simplest.
notes: Order differs between reports (Static then Albright in one; Buck, Static, Albright in the loop write-up). Distance 14.9 vs 15 mi, gain 6,900 vs 7,412 ft. A ski account links Static and Buck via Timberline Lake.

name: Wheeler Peak and Jeff Davis Peak (Doso Doyabi)
region: Snake Range, Great Basin National Park

legs.connect: Walk the ridge south from Wheeler to the saddle, lose several hundred feet, then regain about 400 ft over loose talus; there is no trail.

how: Climb Wheeler by its maintained trail from the scenic-drive trailhead, then keep going along the crest toward the neighbouring summit. The saddle is easy walking and not as exposed as it looks from above, but the far slopes are blocky talus. Wind on the exposed ridge turns many parties around, and the ridge is a poor place to be in a thunderstorm. In winter and spring the same line is skied.
descent: Drop the long talus slope from Doso Doyabi back toward the trees and the trailhead, or return over the ridge. The talus descent is steep and unstable.
logistics: Day trip from the Wheeler Peak Scenic Drive. Wheeler alone gains about 3,000 feet. Start early for afternoon storms; the road may be closed by snow outside summer.
notes: Jeff Davis Peak was officially renamed Doso Doyabi in 2019; both names used in the legs. The 14ers report went past Wheeler toward the second peak but did not state the summit was reached. No class given in any report.

name: Wheeler Peak to Kachina Peak Ridge Traverse
region: Sangre de Cristo Mountains, Taos area

legs.route: Short detour off the Wheeler trail

legs.connect: Continue up the trail from Walter; many parties pass over Walter as a minor bump.
Walk down the ridge from Wheeler; it is a minor bump passed over on the way.
Follow a climbers' trail along the crest.

legs.route: Ridge scramble, crossing the false summit first
legs.connect: Stay on the crest; a short third-class stretch lies near the top.
Continue along the crest, stepping around a large step on the west side.

legs.route: Ridge to the ski area summit
legs.connect: Cross grass and slabby ground to finish above the ski area.

how: After the easy trail to New Mexico's highest summit, the route follows the high crest southwest over six more named summits, several of them minor and unranked. Most of it is class 2 grass and talus. There is third-class scrambling with some exposure between Simpson and Fairchild, and one steep step can be bypassed. Parties may bail down the side basins if weather builds.
descent: Descend from Kachina through the ski area on a marked line and service roads. A shorter version skips Kachina and drops from Lake Fork Peak toward the lake basin and trail.
logistics: Starts at either the Bull of the Woods trail or the Williams Lake trailhead near Taos Ski Valley; the finish is a short way from the start. Roughly 12–16 miles and 4,800–6,000 feet depending on the variation. Summer weather is best; snow lingers late.
notes: Reports differ on whether Walter and Simpson are summited or only passed over, and on start trailhead. One log mentions a cliffed saddle east of a peak.

name: Truchas Peaks Ridge Traverse
region: Sangre de Cristo Mountains, Pecos Wilderness

legs.route: Trail from the Skyline Trail, then the ridge

legs.connect: Descend slightly and climb less than 300 ft; some count this as part of the first summit.
Continue along the crest; the climbers' trail bypasses Middle's top.
Cross a notch and a short steep headwall; pass south of the final peak and finish up it.

duration: 2–3 days (one day from a camp at a lake)
how: Four 13,000-foot summits form one high ridge. Parties camp near a lake basin, then walk the crest between them. Ground is mostly class 1–2 tundra and scree, with class 3 scrambling that varies from mild to very exposed depending on line, and a short class 4 headwall near North Truchas. Direction varies; the order given here runs south to north, and some do it the other way. A trail bypass exists for sections.
descent: Return over a pass to the camp, or drop the north peak by its easy grassy route to the Trampas side. Retracing the ridge is not necessary.
logistics: Common approaches are the Santa Barbara trailhead (camp near the lakes, about 10 miles in) and the Jack's Creek trailhead (about 28 miles round trip in one push). Water is scarce on late-season ridges; early summer has snow but water.
notes: Direction and the order of the middle summits differ by report. Class kept at the higher quoted value (class 4 headwall of about 20 ft). Middle and Medio elevations disagree by a few feet.

name: Gilbert Peak and Gunsight Peak

legs.connect: Descend Gilbert to the saddle and walk south up an expansive slope to Gunsight.

duration: 1 long day or 2–3 days with a camp
how: Both peaks are reached from the Henrys Fork basin. The usual line goes from the trail to Dollar Lake, up a steep grassy ridge to Gilbert, then south along the ridge to Gunsight. The ground is class 2 boulder-hopping with some care on steeper parts and a short scramble near Gilbert's top.
descent: Return the way you came by the saddle. Dropping Gunsight's south face toward the pass is possible but loose scree and cliff bands make it unpleasant.
logistics: About 23 miles and 5,000 feet for the day; many camp at Dollar Lake or at a lake near the trailhead. Summer storms are a risk above timberline.
notes: One report camped at a nearby lake and added another group of peaks on a later day. Gilbert is commonly combined with Kings from the same trailhead but that was not verified from two pages.

name: Tukuhnikivatz, Mount Peale and Mount Mellenthin

legs.route: West ridge from the forest road

legs.connect: Follow the high ridge east; the rock is loose and the going slow.
Continue along the ridge over bumps, some of which can be bypassed.

how: A ridge walk over three summits that rise above a spur road near the pass. Tukuhnikivatz and Peale are done together fairly often; Mellenthin is an easy extension. The ridge is mostly class 2 with class 3 patches; one short section was reported at class 4. Snow in gullies lingers into early summer, and most of the rock is loose talus.
descent: Return along the same ridge and down the west slope to the road, rather than crossing to another trailhead.
logistics: About 9 miles and 4,800 feet round trip from the spur road near Geyser Pass; a longer full traverse from the other end exists. Summer is best.
notes: Order and ridge difficulty differ: one report goes Tuk, Peale, Mellenthin (class 3 at most); the other describes Peale to Mellenthin as class 2 and the Mellenthin to Tuk link as class 4 with the Razor Fang. Class 4 kept as the higher value.
